title: Can Air Duct Cleaning Remove Mold?
h1: Can Air Duct Cleaning Remove Mold Spores?
description: Duct cleaning can remove mold from ducts and registers, but only lasts if the moisture source is fixed. Here is what the process covers and its limits.
quick_answer: Professional duct cleaning can remove mold growth and much of the spore-laden dust from metal ducts, registers and the blower area. It will not keep mold away unless the moisture problem behind it is fixed, and badly affected flexible duct usually needs to be replaced rather than cleaned.
body:
If you've found mold in your ducts or suspect it, cleaning is part of the answer, but not all of it. Mold only grows where there's moisture. If the cleaning crew removes the growth but the moisture stays, it will come back. The best results come from fixing the cause first, then cleaning what's affected.

What can duct cleaning actually remove?

A thorough cleaning uses rotary brushes and strong negative-pressure vacuum to loosen and pull debris out of the duct system. On hard surfaces, it does a good job of removing:

  • Surface mold growth on sheet metal ducts and plenums.
  • Dust and debris that hold mold spores and feed new growth.
  • Buildup on registers, grilles and boots.
  • Debris in the blower compartment and on accessible parts of the system.

After cleaning, an antimicrobial treatment can be applied to the cleaned surfaces where appropriate. It helps, but it's not a substitute for removing the growth and drying out the system.

What can't duct cleaning fix?

The moisture source

Cleaning doesn't stop a clogged condensate line, a rusted drain pan, sweating ducts with torn insulation or a roof leak over the attic. Those need repair, or the mold returns.

Mold inside flexible duct liners

Many San Diego homes use flexible ducts in the attic. Their inner liner is a thin, ribbed plastic that's hard to scrub clean once mold has grown into it, and aggressive brushing can tear it. Affected sections of flex duct are usually better replaced.

Duct board and lined ducts

Some systems use fiberglass duct board or ducts lined with insulation on the inside. Mold that has grown into the fibers can't be fully cleaned out, so those sections may need replacement too.

Mold elsewhere in the house

If mold is growing in walls, under sinks or in the attic, cleaning the ducts won't solve it. The duct system may just be spreading spores from somewhere else.

What does the process look like?

  1. Inspection. We look at the indoor unit, coil, drain pan, plenums and ducts, often with a camera, to see where the growth is and what's causing it.
  2. Fix the moisture. Clear or repair the condensate drain, replace a damaged pan, repair duct insulation or seal leaks.
  3. Contain and clean. The system is put under negative pressure so loosened debris is pulled out instead of blown into the house. Ducts, registers and accessible components are brushed and vacuumed.
  4. Replace what can't be cleaned. Flex duct or lined sections with growth are swapped out.
  5. Treat and verify. Antimicrobial treatment where appropriate, a fresh filter and a final look to confirm the work.

Will cleaning get rid of the musty smell?

Usually, once the growth and the debris are removed and the moisture is under control. If the smell lingers, it may be coming from somewhere the cleaning didn't reach, like the indoor coil, a wall cavity or the attic. A coil cleaning or a closer look elsewhere in the house is the next step.

How do you keep mold from coming back?

  • Keep the condensate drain clear and have it checked during yearly maintenance.
  • Change filters on schedule.
  • Keep indoor humidity in a moderate range. Coastal homes may need a dehumidifier during damp months.
  • Repair torn or thin insulation on attic ducts.
  • Consider a UV light at the indoor coil if mold keeps forming there.

Our air duct cleaning and sanitizing service includes inspection, cleaning and duct repair or replacement when it's needed. For humidity control and UV lights, see our indoor air quality page.

When do you need a mold specialist?

If mold covers a large area, shows up in multiple rooms, or there's water damage inside walls or ceilings, a separate mold assessment may be the right first step. Duct cleaning handles the HVAC side, but it isn't a whole-house mold remediation. If anyone in the home has health concerns, check with a doctor as well.
faqs: Cleaning physically removes mold growth and debris from duct surfaces. An antimicrobial treatment may be applied afterward. The bigger factor is fixing the moisture that let the mold grow in the first place.
How do I know if the mold is gone after cleaning?

The musty smell should fade and visible growth at registers should be gone. A camera inspection after cleaning can confirm the ducts look clear. If the smell returns, the moisture source likely needs more attention.
Can flexible ducts with mold be cleaned?
Usually not well. The thin inner liner is hard to clean once mold grows into it and can tear under brushing, so replacing the affected sections is the more reliable fix.
Should I run my AC if I think there is mold in the ducts?
Running the system can spread spores through the house. If you notice a strong musty smell or visible growth, limit use when possible and schedule an inspection soon.
